luke-evangelist.life: Luke was a companion of the Apostle Paul, whom he joined on Paul's second missionary journey and stayed with when others had left him. He is the author of the Third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, both composed, the sources say, with careful attention to what was known of Christ and the early Church. After the deaths of Peter and Paul he preached in Greece and Egypt, and tradition holds that he died as a martyr at Thebes. Tradition also credits him with the first icons of the Theotokos. Orthocal calls him a physician from Antioch.

demetrios-thessalonica.life: Demetrios was the son of a Roman proconsul at Thessalonica, raised secretly as a Christian. Appointed proconsul after his father, he taught the faith openly instead of persecuting believers. The emperor Maximian had him imprisoned, and in 306 soldiers killed him with lances in his cell. Christians buried his body, and a church was later raised over the grave. Fragrant myrrh was found flowing at his tomb from the seventh century, which gave him the title Myrrh-streamer. He is honored as protector of Thessalonica and is much loved among the Slavs.

synaxis-bodiless-hosts.life: This feast gathers in one commemoration the Archangel Michael, chief of the heavenly hosts, with Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel and the other bodiless powers. The sources tie its establishment to the Council of Laodicea in the fourth century, which affirmed proper veneration of angels while rejecting their worship. November was chosen as the ninth month, matching the nine ranks of angels, and the eighth day recalls the Eighth Day of the age to come. Michael is honored for leading the faithful angels against the rebellion of Lucifer, and the Church asks the help of all the angels.
synaxis-bodiless-hosts.flags: Orthocal also lists the Synaxis of the Holy Unmercenaries on this date; it is not part of the app entry and is not covered. The date of the Laodicea council is given loosely by OCA.

john-chrysostom.life: John was born at Antioch about 347 and raised by his widowed mother, Anthusa. After baptism, a period of monastic life and ordination as presbyter, he preached for years at Antioch, earning the name Chrysostom, the Golden-Mouthed, and left many commentaries and homilies. In 397 he became Archbishop of Constantinople, where he built hospices, reformed the clergy and rebuked the vices of the court. The empress Eudoxia and bishops hostile to him brought about his exile, and he died on the road at Comana on 14 September 407. His relics were returned to Constantinople in 438.
john-chrysostom.flags: The app note mentions St Arcadius of Cyprus on Nov 13; neither the OCA page nor Orthocal for 2026 lists him on this date, so he is not covered. OCA says John's death on 14 September is commemorated on 13 November because of the Elevation of the Cross.

apostle-philip.life: Philip was a native of Bethsaida in Galilee who followed Christ when called and brought Nathanael to Him (John 1). The Gospels also show him at the feeding of the five thousand and at the Last Supper. According to tradition, after the Ascension he preached in Galilee, Greece and Asia Minor with the Apostle Bartholomew and his sister Mariamne. He suffered at Hierapolis in Phrygia, where he was crucified after healing the prefect's wife. Tradition holds an earthquake followed and that Philip prayed for his executioners before he died. He is distinct from Philip the Deacon.
apostle-philip.flags: Orthocal's saints list for Nov 14 also names Gregory Palamas, Justinian and Theodora, and Constantine of Hydra; these are not part of the app entry.

apostle-evangelist-matthew.life: Matthew was a tax collector at Capernaum whom Christ called with the words 'Follow me' (Matthew 9:9). He left his work, made amends for any he had cheated, and became one of the Twelve. The Church holds that he wrote the first Gospel for Jewish believers, originally in Aramaic and later translated into Greek. He then preached in distant lands, and tradition says he ended his ministry in Ethiopia, where he suffered martyrdom. Orthocal places him in Parthia as well, and the sources differ on the details of his later travels.

entrance-theotokos.life: This Great Feast recalls the tradition that Joachim and Anna, keeping a vow made in their childlessness, brought the three-year-old Mary to the Temple in Jerusalem. The High Priest led her into the Holy of Holies, and she remained in the Temple community until her betrothal. The account comes from Church tradition rather than the canonical Gospels, which the Church treats as a sign of her preparation to become the Mother of God. The feast is ancient, with homilies on it from the eighth century, and it opens the approach to the Nativity.

apostle-andrew-first-called.life: Andrew, a fisherman from Bethsaida, was a disciple of John the Baptist and the first to follow Christ, then brought his brother Peter to Him (John 1:35-42). After Pentecost he preached around the Black Sea and in Asia Minor, Thrace and Macedonia, and tradition says he reached the lands of the Slavs. He is held to have founded the Church at Byzantium, so Constantinople honors him as its founder. At Patras in Greece the prefect Aegeatos had him crucified. Andrew taught the crowd from the cross for two days before he died.
apostle-andrew-first-called.place: Bethsaida; Black Sea region; Byzantium; Patras
apostle-andrew-first-called.flags: OCA's page also names Venerable Sebastian Dabovich and Orthocal names Frumentius of Ethiopia on this date; these are not part of the app entry.

sabas-sanctified.life: Sabbas was born in Cappadocia and entered a monastery as a child, then went to Palestine, where he became a disciple of Euthymios the Great. He lived as a hermit in a cave and later, as disciples gathered, founded the Great Lavra near Jerusalem and other monasteries. Church tradition credits him with the first monastic order of services, the Jerusalem Typikon, used across Palestine. He defended the Council of Chalcedon and died in 532 or 533, according to differing sources, having lived over ninety years. His Lavra, Mar Saba, still stands.
sabas-sanctified.flags: OCA gives death 532, Orthocal 533. Orthocal also lists Cosmas the Protos of Athos; not part of the app entry.

nicholas-myra.life: Nicholas was born at Patara in Lycia and became Archbishop of Myra. The sources recall his secret gifts of gold that saved a poor man's daughters, and his imprisonment under Diocletian for the faith. Tradition says he attended the First Ecumenical Council in 325 and opposed Arius, and that he saved three condemned men from execution. He is revered as a protector of travelers and the needy, and a wonderworker. After his death his relics were kept at Myra and then moved to Bari in Italy in 1087. His date of death is not given by OCA.
nicholas-myra.flags: Orthocal also lists New Martyr Nicolas Karamos and Maximus of Kiev; not part of the app entry. Death year (345 in Orthocal) is not stated by OCA and is omitted.

spyridon-trimythous.life: Spyridon was a shepherd on Cyprus, married with children, whose generosity to the poor and travelers was said to be rewarded with the gift of healing. After his wife died he was made Bishop of Tremithus in the time of Constantine. He took part in the First Ecumenical Council in 325, where tradition says he led a philosopher to the faith and illustrated the Trinity with a brick. He is remembered for hospitality and many miracles. His relics rest in the church dedicated to him on Corfu.
spyridon-trimythous.flags: App note gives death as +348; neither OCA nor Orthocal states a death year, so it is omitted. OCA spells the see Tremithus and also lists Mardarije of Libertyville (not in the app entry).

forefeast-nativity-eve.life: The eve of the Nativity, called the Paramone, is the last day of preparation before the feast of Christ's birth. A strict fast is kept. In Slavic practice the Church serves the Royal Hours, then Vespers joined to the Liturgy of Saint Basil. At Vespers eight Old Testament readings are read, and the Gospel is carried in at the entrance. At the end of the Liturgy a lighted candle is placed in the center of the church and the troparion and kontakion of the feast are sung. The Vigil follows with Great Compline and Matins.
forefeast-nativity-eve.flags: Orthocal lists the Eve of Nativity and Martyr Eugenia; Eugenia is not part of the app entry. The OCA text describes services only, with no narrative; the app's rank-1 treatment is the app's own choice.

nativity-christ.life: The Nativity of Christ commemorates His birth of the Virgin Mary at Bethlehem during the reign of Caesar Augustus, when Mary and Joseph went there for the census. Luke's Gospel tells how He was laid in a manger and how an angel announced the news to shepherds; Matthew tells of the Magi, who followed a star and brought gifts. The sources show the feast was kept in the early Church, and by the fourth century widely. Its hymns continue through the days that follow.

synaxis-theotokos-nativity.life: On the day after the Nativity the Church gathers, the meaning of 'synaxis', to honor the Virgin Mary, through whom the Incarnation took place. OCA describes it as probably the oldest feast of Mary, and notes that Epiphanios of Cyprus was already preaching on it in the fourth century. In earlier calendars the day also recalled the Magi's gifts and the flight into Egypt, and the Flight is still commemorated now. It is the second day of the three-day festal celebration of the Nativity, and the Nativity hymns are joined with praise of the Theotokos.
synaxis-theotokos-nativity.flags: Orthocal also lists the Flight into Egypt, Euthymius of Sardis and Constantine of Synnada; these are not part of the app entry.

protomartyr-stephen.life: Stephen was the eldest of the seven deacons appointed by the Apostles, and so is called archdeacon. Acts 6 and 7 tell how he preached Christ with great power, was accused before the Sanhedrin and gave a long speech. While speaking he saw the heavens open and Christ standing at God's right hand. He was dragged out of Jerusalem and stoned, praying for his killers, and so became the first Christian martyr. Tradition says Gamaliel buried his body. His commemoration falls on the third day of the Nativity festal period.
protomartyr-stephen.flags: In 2026 Dec 27 is a Sunday; OCA's page leads with David, Joseph and James of the Sunday after Nativity, with Stephen second. Orthocal lists Stephen as the feast.
